Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s overall position

**Do not accept this package as “standard”, “FINAL” or already agreed merely because Seller’s counsel says so.** Confirm any actual principal-level approvals against the Buyer’s own records. The review restrictions in the Seller’s documents are not a reason to leave buyer-adverse terms unchallenged.

The principal concerns are **completion without critical consent or clean security releases; unallocated debt and transaction costs; uncertain IP ownership; and limitations that could undermine almost every Buyer remedy.**

This review is based on the supplied summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying DD documents or full SPA. Proposed drafting must be checked against those documents.

## 1. Completion conditions and purchase-price protection

### Bluefen: written consent alone is insufficient

Bluefen accounts for approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. The Disclosure Letter expressly says neither final consent nor evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions has been provided.

**Push back:**
- Make effective Bluefen change-of-control consent a Buyer-waivable condition precedent—not merely a reasonable-endeavours obligation.
- Require compliance with relevant clause 11.3 conditions and evidence that consent is operative at Completion.
- Require Buyer approval of any concessions, fees, revised commercial terms or continuing conditions.
- Provide an appropriate longstop and termination right if the condition is not satisfied.

**Why:** Delivery of a document labelled “consent” does not protect the acquired revenue if it remains conditional, ineffective or commercially damaging.

### Riverlark: no unsecured promise of a post-Completion release

The approximately **AUD 3.2 million facility remains outstanding**, with no final security discharge. A release “following Completion” exposes the Buyer to financing, enforcement and change-of-control risk.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a lender payout statement and agreed Completion discharge arrangements covering all relevant security, guarantees and other obligations.
- Pay the lender directly through the Completion funds flow, with effective releases at Completion or tightly controlled simultaneous arrangements backed by binding lender undertakings.
- Deal expressly with interest, break costs and discharge fees.
- Confirm the price bridge implements the agreed **debt-free/cash-free** bargain, without double counting.

**Why:** Buying the shares does not itself remove company debt or security. Clarify whether AUD 24 million is the enterprise-value reference or the equity payment before approving the funds flow.

### Completion bonuses: allocate the actual cost

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are triggered by Completion and continued-employment conditions but omitted from the funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the Company bearing them.

**Push back:**
- Confirm the obligor, recipients, conditions and payment dates.
- Expressly allocate the agreed Seller-borne amounts through payment, a price deduction or a specific indemnity.
- Quantify applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs.
- Ensure the amount is not omitted—or counted twice—between debt-like items, transaction expenses and working capital.

**Why:** Otherwise the Buyer may fund an undisclosed acquisition-related cash outflow immediately after Completion.

## 2. Known risks need substantive protection—not disclosure alone

### Ironquay: payment exposure is not the whole IP risk

The materials indicate that transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open, but actual payment status and ownership remain unverified.

**Push back:**
- Obtain payment reconciliation, bank evidence and Ironquay confirmation.
- Require cleared settlement and a confirmatory assignment or other sufficient chain-of-title documentation at or before Completion.
- Verify the relevant IP rights, contributors and any necessary licences.
- Broaden the indemnity beyond the invoice to cover losses arising from the identified ownership defect, including third-party claims and reasonable remediation costs.
- Keep that indemnity outside inappropriate general warranty limitations.

**Why:** An indemnity limited to paying an invoice may leave the Buyer without essential IP rights or adequate compensation for disruption. Do not assert non-payment or missing ownership as established facts yet.

### Export/privacy incident: investigate before pricing or accepting the risk

The disclosure establishes a misdirected download link, **not a confirmed unauthorised access event or notifiable breach**. Equally, the Seller’s “not expected to be material” assertion is unsupported by the preliminary record.

**Push back:**
- Require prompt investigation of access logs, link permissions, duration, recipients, data scope and containment.
- Assess applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations.
- Require updates through Completion, preservation of evidence and appropriate consultation over notifications and remediation, without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a tailored indemnity for the pre-Completion incident, with appropriate duration and security if warranted.

**Why:** Uncertainty is not a reason to treat the exposure as immaterial. Potential costs extend beyond immediate financial loss.

### Sandbar renewals: examine the aggregate commitment

The three renewals total **AUD 330,000**. Neither “ordinary course” nor unavoidable liability is established.

**Push back:**
- Read DD-008 and DD-011 together and establish commitment dates, renewal periods, termination rights, accruals and commercial necessity.
- Apply interim-conduct approval thresholds to related transactions in aggregate.
- Determine the correct economic treatment from the facts.

**Why:** These may be normal future operating expenses, existing liabilities or exceptional commitments. They should neither automatically reduce the price nor automatically escape scrutiny.

## 3. Rework the liability architecture

| Seller position | Buyer objection and recommended response |
|---|---|
| **General warranty cap: AUD 4.8m / 20%** | Not automatically unacceptable, but adequacy depends on diligence, warranty coverage and recoverability. Negotiate it as part of the whole package—not as a ceiling for all risks. |
| **AUD 25,000 de minimis; AUD 250,000 excess-only basket** | Together these leave meaningful losses with Buyer. Seek lower thresholds and a tipping basket. Aggregate connected claims; clarify whether the de minimis excludes entire claims or only part of them. |
| **18-month notification period** | May expire before latent problems emerge. Seek a longer general period covering sufficient reporting cycles, with materially longer, separately negotiated periods for tax and fundamental warranties. Preserve properly notified claims until resolved. |
| **Title/capacity under general cap and time limit** | Reject. Seek a separate cap at least equal to the purchase price, no general basket/de minimis and a substantially longer claim period, subject to applicable law. Defective title could undermine the entire acquisition. |
| **Tax and IP under the general regime** | Negotiate tax-specific warranties and an indemnity/covenant for pre-Completion tax, with suitable statutory-assessment-period coverage and procedural protections. Assess separate IP protection given its importance to this SaaS business and the identified issue. |
| **All limitations apply to all Claims** | Reject blanket application. Expressly distinguish general warranties, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, payment obligations, completion adjustments and covenant breaches. Specify which limitations apply to each. |
| **Universal exclusive-remedy/non-reliance provisions** | Preserve agreed indemnities, debt and payment recovery, adjustment mechanisms, appropriate equitable relief, fraud-related claims and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Review the actual wording under NSW law; do not assume contractual wording can exclude every statutory remedy. |

**Why the package matters:** A superficially acceptable cap offers little protection if disclosure, knowledge exclusions, short deadlines and exclusive remedies eliminate the underlying claim first. Also assess Seller creditworthiness and whether escrow, retention or other security is needed.

## 4. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge are excessively broad

### Blanket data-room disclosure

Disclosing everything “contained or referred to” in the room, accounts and public records risks treating buried, incomplete or externally referenced material as an effective warranty exception.

**Push back:**
- Require fair disclosure with enough detail to identify the nature and scope of the exception.
- Link specific disclosures to relevant warranties, with tightly controlled cross-application.
- Reject blanket incorporation of unidentified referenced material.
- Identify and preserve the exact disclosed data-room set.
- Require updates from **22 September 2026** through signing and Completion; later disclosure should not automatically remove Buyer remedies.

Disclosure is **not** consent, repayment, assignment, remediation or an agreed allocation of loss. Known matters requiring protection should have express obligations or indemnities that survive their disclosure.

### Buyer/adviser knowledge

“Discoverable” matters create an exceptionally broad constructive-knowledge defence.

**Push back:**
- Delete the knowledge exclusion if possible.
- If retained, restrict it to actual knowledge of specifically named Buyer personnel, with no deemed knowledge, duty of inquiry or automatic attribution from advisers.
- Ensure agreed specific indemnities remain effective despite Buyer knowledge.

**Why:** Access to documents is not the same as appreciating an actionable defect. The Seller should not transfer the risk of its warranties being false simply because diligence was possible.

## 5. Avoid unsupported consent and title conclusions

- **Office lease:** The supplied material identifies a notification obligation, not landlord consent. Verify and comply with the notice requirement; do not invent a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not, without more, establish a share-sale consent requirement. Check the complete contract for change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording.
- **Share title:** DD-012 is relevant evidence, not conclusive verification of clean, transferable ownership. Check share capital history, certificates, encumbrances, options and other rights, transfer restrictions, approvals and Completion transfer mechanics.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure Completion:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark payoff and releases, and satisfactory Ironquay ownership evidence.
2. **Fix the economics:** reconcile debt-free/cash-free pricing, bonuses and on-costs, and supplier commitments.
3. **Preserve meaningful remedies:** separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; narrow universal limitations, disclosure and knowledge exclusions.
4. **Resolve uncertainty:** investigate the export incident and update diligence through Completion.
5. **Verify approvals and title:** do not accept Seller labels or the share register as substitutes for Buyer verification.

**Bottom line:** The Seller’s package combines unresolved business risks with provisions that could leave those risks largely unrecoverable. Negotiate the completion protections, economic allocation and remedy structure together.
